terms.grammar: verb, second conjugation, semi-deponent, with an infinitive
evidence: Verg. A. 6.14–15: Daedalus … ausus sē crēdere caelō
terms.comment: The perfect is passive in form: ausus sum, I dared. The old subjunctive ausim, “I would dare”, is found in comedy, in the poets, and in Livy’s preface (Lewis & Short). Cicero explains sōdēs, “please”, as sī audēs, “if you will” (Or. 154, cited by Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: dīmidium factī, quī coepit, habet; sapere audē, incipe
phrases.english: well begun is half done: dare to be wise, make a start

phrases.latin: Daedalus, ut fāma est, … praepetibus pennīs ausus sē crēdere caelō
phrases.english: Daedalus, so the story goes, … dared to trust himself to the sky on swift wings
Who would dare to call the sun a liar?

phrases.latin: nec satis sciō nec, sī sciam, dīcere ausim
phrases.english: I don’t really know, and if I did, I wouldn’t dare say
I wouldn’t dare bet anything against you

phrases.latin: quid dulcius quam habēre quīcum omnia audeās sīc loquī ut tēcum?
phrases.english: what is sweeter than having someone you dare speak to about everything as if to yourself?

sources: Lewis & Short: audeo · Lewis & Short: sodes
